name: Lahore
info: Lahore is a city on the Ravi River in the Punjab of Pakistan, first named in a document of 982, a capital of the Ghaznavids, the Mughals under Akbar and the Sikh Empire, and now the capital of Pakistan's province of Punjab.

facts.founded: No definitive record of its founding exists. Oral tradition says Lava, son of Rama, founded it; the first document to name the city is the Hudud al-'Alam of 982.
facts.where: In central-eastern Punjab, along the Ravi River, in north-eastern Pakistan close to the border with India.
facts.known: The Odi Shahi, Ghaznavid and Mamluk capital; the Mughal capital under Akbar; the Lahore Fort, the Badshahi Mosque and the Shalimar Gardens; the capital of Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire; the Lahore Resolution of 1940; the riots of Partition in 1947
facts.today: Lahore is the capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab and the second-largest city of Pakistan, with a population of over 14 million.

t: Lahore rose to prominence in the late 10th century and served as a capital under the Odi Shahi dynasty, the Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals under Akbar and the Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh.

Its Mughal monuments, among them the Lahore Fort, the Shalimar Gardens and the Badshahi Mosque, were built between the reigns of Akbar and Aurangzeb, and the city decayed in the 18th century under repeated Afghan, Maratha and Sikh contests.

The East India Company annexed Punjab in 1849, the Lahore Resolution of 1940 called for Pakistan, and the city suffered the worst riots of Partition in 1947 before becoming the capital of Pakistani Punjab.
dyk: The Badshahi Mosque, raised in 1673 under Aurangzeb, was the largest mosque in the world when it was built.
ev: The Hudud al-'Alam, the first document to name Lahore, describes a town with impressive temples, large markets and huge orchards
Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni conquers Lahore and makes it part of the Ghaznavid Empire
The Mongol army sacks and ruins the city
Akbar begins re-fortifying the citadel and makes Lahore the Mughal capital
Ranjit Singh captures Lahore and makes it the capital of the Sikh Empire
Punjab is annexed to the British Indian Empire and Lahore becomes the capital of the province
The All India Muslim League passes the Lahore Resolution demanding a separate homeland for the Muslims of India
Riots in the weeks of Partition end with Lahore awarded to Pakistan on 17 August

sections.origins:
Lahore lies on the Ravi River in central-eastern Punjab. No definitive record of its early history exists, and its unclear background has given rise to several theories about its establishment. Oral tradition holds that the city was named after Lava, son of the Hindu god Rama, who supposedly founded it, and the Lahore Fort has a vacant temple dedicated to Lava. The origin of the name is otherwise unclear. Early Muslim historians recorded it as Luhawar, Luhar and Rahwar, and one theory derives it from Ravawar, a name possibly drawn from the Ravi, known as the Iravati in the Vedas. Another theory derives it from the word lohar, meaning blacksmith.

The historians of Alexander the Great mention no city near the site during his invasion in 326 BCE, which suggests that it had not been founded or was not noteworthy. Ptolemy mentions in his Geography a city called Labokla near the Chenab and Ravi, which may have been ancient Lahore or an abandoned predecessor of it. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described a large and prosperous unnamed city when he visited the region in 630 CE, and it may have been Lahore.

The first document to mention Lahore by name is the Hudud al-'Alam, written in 982. It describes a town with impressive temples, large markets and huge orchards. Before the Ghaznavid conquest in the 11th century, Lahore appears to have been the capital of Punjab under the maharaja Anandapala of the Odi Shahi dynasty, who moved his capital there from Udabhandapura.
sections.growth:
Under the Ghaznavids Lahore became a cultural and academic centre renowned for poetry, and poets and scholars from other cities of the empire gathered there. Under the Mamluk sultan Qutb ud-Din Aibak it attracted poets and scholars from the medieval Muslim world, and it had more poets writing in Persian than any other city. Its greatest prosperity came under the Mughals, and it has more Mughal monuments than either Delhi or Agra. The Tughluq ruler Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq saw it flourish briefly between 1320 and 1325.

In Akbar's time most residents lived in suburbs outside the walls, and only 9 of the 36 urban quarters, known as guzars, lay inside them. Akbar rebuilt the walls, extended them east of the Shah Alami bazaar, set up the Akbari Mandi grain market and established the Dharampura neighbourhood. Shah Jahan, born in Lahore in 1592, renovated the fort in white marble, built the Naulakha Pavilion in 1633 and laid out the Shalamar Gardens in 1641. The population of pre-modern Lahore probably reached its peak in his reign, with perhaps six times as many people in the suburbs as in the Walled City. Aurangzeb built the Alamgiri Bund along the Ravi in 1662, the Badshahi Mosque in 1673 and the Alamgiri Gate of the fort in 1674.

Under British rule the city grew south of the Walled City. Model Town was established as a garden suburb in 1921. An estimated 200,000 people lived in Lahore in 1901.
sections.rulers:
The city was the capital of the Odi Shahi maharaja Anandapala before Sultan Mahmud conquered it between 1020 and 1027 and made it part of the Ghaznavid Empire. It became the eastern capital of the Ghaznavids in 1152 and their sole capital after the fall of Ghazni in 1163. The Ghurid ruler Muhammad captured it after the siege of 1186, and after his assassination in 1206 it was the first capital of the Mamluk dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Delhi's sultans later preferred Delhi as a safer capital, and the city passed between the Delhi Sultanate, the Khwarazmian ruler Jalal al-Din Mangburni, the Mongols, the Khokhars and Timur, who took it in 1398.

Babur captured Lahore in 1525, and Humayun reconquered it in February 1555 after the interval of Sher Shah Suri. From 1584 Akbar made it the Mughal capital. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 its governors held it for ever weaker emperors, Nader Shah invaded in 1739, and Ahmad Shah Durrani occupied it in 1748 and invaded again in 1751, 1752 and 1757. The Marathas occupied it in 1758, and the Durranis withdrew in 1765. The Bhangi Misl captured it in 1767, and in 1780 it was divided among three rulers.

Ranjit Singh took Lahore in 1799 and made it the administrative capital of the Sikh Empire. The East India Company seized it in February 1846, and Punjab was annexed in 1849. It remained the capital of the province under British rule until 1947.
sections.life:
Lahore's Walled City was built piecemeal, with small cul-de-sacs, as katrahs and galis developed beside neighbouring buildings, and it had thirteen gates. Some neighbourhoods were named for a religious or ethnic community, but they were typically diverse and not dominated by it. The bazaars of the old city included the Sarafa, Copper and Brass, Kashmiri and Shah Alami bazaars. In the late Mughal period the city was closely tied to market towns such as Kasur and Eminabad and to Amritsar and Batala.

Several faiths left marks on the city. According to one account, Jainism was the oldest religion of Punjab, and Jain temples stood at places still called Thari Bhabrian and Gali Bhabrian. Lahore's first church was built under Akbar in the late 16th century and levelled by Shah Jahan in 1632. Sufi shrines, among them that of Ali al-Hujwiri at the Data Darbar and that of Mian Mir, hold annual festivals called urs. Lahore also contains some of the holiest sites of Sikhism, including the Gurdwara Dera Sahib, built to mark the site of Guru Arjan Dev's death in 1606.

The city was a centre of Persian letters. In the 17th century the Lahore Quartet of Abu al-Barakat Munir Lahori, Muhammad Saleh Kamboh, Shaikh Inayat Allah Kamboh and Chandar Bhan Brahman, four local scholars and poets, promoted one another and revived Persian literacy in India. The British laid out their Civil Station south of the Walled City, where British and locals mixed along The Mall, and the Cantonment, where laws against mixing existed.
sections.crises:
Lahore was devastated by the Ghaznavid invasion, and Malik Ayaz rebuilt and repopulated it. A Mongol army sacked and ruined it in 1241, and Mongol attacks followed in 1287, 1298 and 1305. Tarmashirin sacked it in 1329. By the time Timur took it in 1398 he did not loot it, because it was no longer wealthy. Babur sacked it in 1525. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the city declined: Nader Shah's invasion in 1739 shifted trade routes away from it, the Indus ports that served it silted up, and it had nine different governors between 1745 and 1756. By the end of the 18th century its remaining people lived inside the walls while the suburbs lay abandoned.

The partition of British India in 1947 brought the worst riots of Partition to Lahore, as the city's fate was fiercely contested. The 1941 census counted 671,659 people, 64.5 per cent of them Muslim and about 35 per cent Hindu and Sikh. Hindus and Sikhs disputed these figures before the Boundary Commission and argued that the city was only 54 per cent Muslim; two thirds of its shops and 80 per cent of its factories belonged to Hindus and Sikhs. Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs were all both victims and perpetrators. The riots of March and April 1947 destroyed 6,000 of Lahore's 82,000 homes, and violence rose through the summer despite British armoured personnel. By late August 66 per cent of Hindus and Sikhs had left, and the Shah Alami Bazaar, once a largely Hindu quarter, was burnt down. On 17 August Lahore was awarded to Pakistan.
sections.legacy:
The Lahore Fort and the Shalimar Gardens are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Ranjit Singh's rule restored some of the city's lost standing but his armies plundered Mughal monuments for building materials and stripped the marble of the Tomb of Asif Khan, the Tomb of Nur Jahan and the Shalimar Gardens. The Badshahi Mosque was used as an ammunition depot and a stable. Ranjit Singh built the Hazuri Bagh Baradari in 1818 and a gurdwara marking Guru Ram Das's birthplace in 1801. In 1841 Sher Singh's soldiers placed guns on the minarets of the Badshahi Mosque and destroyed the fort's Diwan-e-Aam. The British built the Lahore Museum and the Mayo School of Industrial Arts in the Indo-Saracenic style around 1887, and Sir Ganga Ram, called the father of modern Lahore, designed many of its important buildings.

Lahore was central to the independence movements. Nehru moved the Declaration of Independence of India at Bradlaugh Hall on 31 December 1929, Bhagat Singh was hanged in the city's jail in 1931, and the Muslim League passed the Lahore Resolution in 1940. After Partition its industrial production fell to one third of its earlier level and Karachi, not Lahore, became the capital. Lahore was capital of West Pakistan from 1955 until 1970, and the Minar-e-Pakistan was completed in 1968 where the resolution was passed. The Walled City restoration began in 2009.

summary: Lahore, on the Ravi in Pakistani Punjab, was first named in 982 and served as a capital of the Ghaznavids, Akbar's Mughals and Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire. Its Partition riots of 1947 preceded its award to Pakistan, and it is now the capital of Punjab province.
references: William Glover, Making Lahore Modern, Constructing and Imagining a Colonial City (University of Minnesota Press, 2008)
Syad Muhammad Latif, Lahore: Its History, Architectural Remains and Antiquities (New Imperial Press, 1892)
notes: START: no founding date exists in either article; the first document naming the city is the Hudud al-'Alam of 982, so start is 982 with circa true. The main article says the site was inhabited for over two millennia but gives no date.

DISAGREEMENT, Ghaznavid conquest: the main article says Mahmud conquered Lahore between 1020 and 1027 and appointed Malik Ayaz governor in 1021; the history article says Mahmud seized it in 1022 and in 1021 appointed Malik Ayaz 'to the throne' and made Lahore the Ghaznavid capital. I used '1020s' and 'between 1020 and 1027' and left out 1021, 1022 and the history article's 'capital' claim (the main article makes Lahore an eastern capital only in 1152).

DISAGREEMENT, Mongols 1241: the main article says the army sacked and ruined the city and held it for a few years under Toghrul; the history article says 30,000 cavalry massacred the entire population and levelled the city, and that no building predates this. I used the main article's wording and left out the massacre and the 30,000.
DISAGREEMENT, Ghurid capture: 1186 (main) against 1187 (history). I used 1186.
DISAGREEMENT, Babur: the main article has 1525, the history article gives 1524 as the start of Mughal rule and a battle of Panipat in 1526. I used 1525 only.
DISAGREEMENT, Akbar's capital: main article 'beginning in 1584'; history article says Akbar and Jahangir 1584 to 1598. I used 1584 only.

DISAGREEMENT, Ranjit Singh's capture: the main article does not date it beyond 'in the aftermath of Zaman Shah's 1799 invasion' with the gate tradition; the history article says 7 July 1799. I used 1799. The main article's timeline gives the Sikh Empire 1765-1799 and the text says Bhangi Misl took it in 1767 (history: 1765, and Bhangi leader entered in 1765); I wrote 'from 1765' and 'in 1767' as each article has them. Check.

Durrani invasions: 1748, 1751, 1752, 1757 (four conquests per the main article, which lists 1748, 1751, 1752, 1756-57); I wrote 'in 1748 and in four further invasions up to 1757', which is not exactly what the article says (it says conquered a third time in 1752 and a fourth time invaded in 1757). EDITOR: rewrite or check.
Nine governors: the main article does not give it; the history article says nine governors between 1745 and 1756, which I wrote as 'in the 1740s ... eleven years' (a derived span). Check.

Sher Singh's soldiers and the Diwan-e-Aam: both articles; the main says 14 January 1841. History article says 'inflicting great damage' to the fort; the main says the Diwan-e-Aam was destroyed. Used the main.

Badshahi Mosque 'largest mosque in the world upon construction' is from the Tourism section of the main article; the date is 1673 there and in Architecture (also 1673 in the history article's period of Aurangzeb).

Partition: the articles give no death toll. The main article says 'carnage' with all three groups both victims and perpetrators. The history article says 'many deaths' and damage to the Lahore Fort and Badshahi Mosque, which the main article does not say; left out. The Radcliffe anecdote (Nayar's claim of 1971) was left out as a claim of a single journalist.

Jain heritage: the history article says Plutarch 'and many other scholars suggest' Jainism was the most ancient religion in Punjab; I wrote 'According to one account'. The Lohana derivation was left out as garbled.

Left out as contested or garbled in the history article: the 'Ancient era' Hindu heritage date of 580 BC, the 682 AD Afghan wars and Ferishta's story of Jayapala and Sabuktigin (975), the Rajputana chronicles, the Hindu forced conversions sentence, the 'Hindu Shahis' dates, the Taank Kingdom timeline.

The population estimate 120,000 at the start of British rule was not used; 1901 estimate of 200,000 used. 'Over 14 million' is the main article's lead figure without a year; 2017 census figure 11,126,285 is not used.
The 'Late Mughal' decline sentences: 'the trade routes had shifted away from Lahore, and south towards Kandahar' is paraphrased as shifting away.

Wording check for the editor: 'Under the Crown it remained the capital of the province until 1947' uses the main article's 'British Raj / British Empire 1858-1947' and 'capital of Punjab Province' after 1849; 'Crown' is not in the articles, consider changing to 'British rule'.
Also left out as tourism, sport, transport, economy and government sections; the 1965 war, the 1992 riots and the 1974 summit (kept the 1955-1970 West Pakistan capital).
